issues.legal_issue: A family member’s genealogy testimony and properly kept genealogical records may be admissible and sufficient evidence to support a finding of family relationship and reversionary status.
material_facts: A family member testified to the genealogy, relying partly on information acquired from deceased relatives, and expressed an independent opinion formed through family conduct.

Professional genealogists maintained pedigree records in the ordinary course of their work; the records were proved, came from proper custody, and included entries made by deceased persons other than the testifying family member.
Some records were proved through testimony given in an earlier proceeding.
Both lower courts found the plaintiffs to be the next reversioners, and the challenge to that finding turned on the legal admissibility of the evidence.
issues.conclusion: The family member’s testimony was admissible and, if believed, legally sufficient to support the finding. The genealogical records made by persons other than that witness were admissible under Sections 32(2) and 32(6) of the Evidence Act; testimony from the earlier proceeding was admissible under Section 33. Taken together, the testimony and records sufficiently supported the concurrent finding, and the challenge to it failed.
issues.legal_principle: A family member may testify to family relationships based on information learned from deceased persons if the testimony expresses the witness’s own independent opinion and that opinion is expressed by conduct; the sources and timing of the information affect weight, not admissibility. Under Sections 32(2) and 32(6) of the Evidence Act, genealogical entries made by deceased persons may be relevant as statements made in the ordinary course of business or concerning family relationship. Section 32(2) does not require that an entry predate the dispute. Prior testimony may be admissible under Section 33. The cited authorities are Mohansing v. Dalpatsing, AIR 1922 Bom 51, and Abdul Ghafur v. Hussain Bibi. A concurrent factual finding cannot be challenged on appeal unless the evidence on which it rests is legally inadmissible.

rule.if: genealogy_relationship_proceeding and family_member_independent_opinion and genealogical_records_kept_in_ordinary_business and genealogical_records_properly_proved and earlier_proceeding_testimony_used

predicates.genealogy_relationship_proceeding: The proceeding concerned a claim to succession that depended on disputed family relationships.
predicates.family_member_independent_opinion: A family member testified to ancestry using information learned from deceased relatives and expressed an independent opinion about the relationships, with that opinion expressed through conduct.
predicates.genealogical_records_kept_in_ordinary_bu: Professional genealogists maintained pedigree records as part of their ordinary work, including entries made by persons who had since died.
predicates.genealogical_records_properly_proved: The genealogical records were proved and produced from proper custody.
predicates.earlier_proceeding_testimony_used: Testimony given in an earlier proceeding was used to prove some genealogical records.

issues.definition: When a succession dispute turns on family relationships, this rule treats the described family testimony and genealogical records, including relevant prior testimony, as admissible and sufficient to support a relationship finding.

issues.legal_issue: Property purchased by a widow with savings from the income of her husband’s estate does not become part of that estate merely because the income came from it; the widow’s intention determines whether she kept the property separate or added it to the estate.
material_facts: The widow purchased the disputed properties with savings from income derived from her husband’s estate.
The properties had not come to the widow from her husband and had been purchased by her.
The widow later dedicated the properties to family deities, stating in the deed that she acted in accordance with her husband’s wishes.
The claimants produced no evidence indicating that the widow intended to add the properties to her husband’s estate.
issues.conclusion: The claimants did not establish that the properties formed part of the husband’s estate. The widow intended to keep them separate, so the claim to those properties failed.
issues.legal_principle: A reversioner may claim only property that belonged to the propositus, and the claimant bears the burden of establishing that a particular property held by the widow formed part of that estate. There is no presumption that property in a widow’s hands belonged to her husband. A Hindu widow has an absolute right to income from her husband’s estate and need not save it for reversioners; she may add the savings to the estate or keep them separate and deal with them as her own. The question is one of intention and is a question of fact. The Court relied on Venkatadri Appa Rao v. Parthasarathi Appa Rao, at pages 108–109; Babu Sheo Lochun Singh v. Babu Saheb Singh, 14 Ind App 63 (PC); and Raja of Ramnad v. Sundara Pandiyasami Tevar, AIR 1918 PC 156.

predicates.reversioner_claim_to_widow_held_property: A claimant asserting a right as a reversioner sought property that had been held by a widow.
predicates.widow_purchased_property_from_estate_inc: The widow purchased the property using savings from income derived from her husband’s estate.
predicates.widow_dedicated_property_separately: The widow dedicated the purchased property to family deities, indicating that she dealt with it separately.
predicates.no_evidence_of_intent_to_add_property_to: The claimant produced no evidence that the widow intended to add the purchased property to her husband’s estate.

issues.definition: When a reversioner claims property purchased by a widow from savings of estate income, separate dedication without evidence of an intention to add the property to the estate means the property is not established as part of the husband’s estate.
